transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-07 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Solutions), Ethan Morales (Head of ML - Frostbyte), Priya Nair (Platform Eng), Samir Kaur (CTO), Alex Ruiz (SRE)

---
00:00:03 Jordan: Hey, everyone. Thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. Quick intro, Maya is our SE who will drive the technical bits. Um, do you want to kick off, Ethan?
00:00:12 Ethan: Yeah sure. Uh thanks. We're Frostbyte Labs, we build ML inference for genomic analysis pipelines. We're looking at moving some of our heavy batch + interactive workloads off our in-house cluster and considering Redwood Dedicated or a private install. Goal is to get predictable latency for our interactive UI but also have reserved throughput for nightly batch jobs.
00:00:33 Maya: Great, can you give a rough sense of current concurrency and token sizes? That helps us size prewarms.
00:00:39 Ethan: Typical interactive is like 200 concurrent users, p95 latency target around 200-300ms for short prompts (1-2k tokens). Nightly batches are huge—jobs that spin up 10-20k token sequences but can tolerate higher latency.
00:00:53 Priya: For us the big thing is isolation. We can't have noisy neighbors affecting batch latency during peak office hours. Also key is KMS integration and audit logs for compliance.
00:01:04 Jordan: Totally. On isolation we support tenant-fenced Dedicated pools — reserved GPUs dedicated just to you — and we can configure eviction/priority policies. Also we offer Private deployment for full on-prem or VPC control with customer-managed KMS.
00:01:18 Samir: For compliance, are you SOC2 and ISO certified? And how do audit logs work with Private vs Hosted?
00:01:25 Maya: Redwood holds SOC2 Type II for Hosted control plane; our Private package mirrors the same audit logging surface but logs are forwarded to your SIEM. For KMS, if you choose Private we can hook into your HSM or cloud KMS, keys never leave your tenancy.
00:01:40 Alex: Is there a difference in performance between Private and Dedicated-hosted? I ask bc our ops folks are worried about networking overhead for VPC egress to a hosted control plane.
00:01:49 Liam: Good question. The runtime can be colocated in your region. Dedicated (hosted) offers lower friction — we manage infra — while Private on VPC/on‑prem gives you more control but can add a small network hop. Typically we see <5% perf delta in properly peered VPCs, but on‑prem setups depend on your network.
00:02:07 Ethan: Okay. What about burst? Our traffic has sudden spikes when a new dataset drops. We need a plan to handle 3x baseline concurrency for short windows (10–15 minutes) without a huge cost hit.
00:02:18 Maya: Two main patterns: warm/hot pools + burst elastics. With Dedicated you reserve baseline nodes and can configure burst capacity as transient instances that spin up quickly; prewarm strategies (hot pool) keep a small set of GPUs ready to reduce cold-start. We also support controlled fallbacks to hosted model variants if you hit capacity.
00:02:37 Priya: How quick is spin-up for burst nodes? We've seen cloud GPUs take several minutes in other providers.
:02:41 Ethan: (overlap) yeah that's a concern.
00:02:43 Maya: Our burst path can start pre-provisioned hot-pools which are warmed kernels ready to go, so effective spin-up is on the order of 20-90s depending on model size and KV cache priming. For fully cold VMs it can be minutes. So we recommend a hybrid: small hot pool for interactive traffic and elastics for extended surges.
00:03:02 Jordan: And you can set burst budgets by tokens or session counts so cost stays predictable.
00:03:08 Samir: Can the hot pool be isolated to specific models? We run both large Llama‑style models for generative summaries and smaller rerankers.
00:03:16 Maya: Yes, hot-pools are configured per deployment/model family. We can pin quantized variants to hot pools to reduce memory and warm time.
00:03:25 Priya: Speaking of quantization, will that affect quality? We have strict accuracy needs for clinical-allele calls.
00:03:31 Maya: There's always a small delta. Our Optimize tool can recommend quantization profiles and run A/B tests. For clinical-critical paths you might keep fp16/vocab full-precision models on dedicated nodes and use quantized models for lower-risk routes.
00:03:46 Ethan: Ok good. Let's talk about routing behavior — if Dedicated is at capacity during a spike, can requests fail over to Hosted? We cannot lose availability for client-facing features.
00:03:57 Liam: Yes, smart routing policies allow failover to compatible hosted model variants with either slower latency or reduced throughput. You can configure strict or permissive fallthrough and rate caps. We also provide circuit-breakers and staged rollouts.
00:04:12 Alex: Any security concerns when failing over to hosted? Data residency and PHI are concerns for us.
00:04:19 Maya: For PHI/regulated data we recommend Private or Dedicated with strict VPC egress rules; failover to Hosted should be limited for non-PII paths. Also you can mask or tokenize sensitive payloads before sending.
00:04:30 Samir: Ok that helps. Another practical question: how do you measure token billing for batch vs interactive? We need cost predictability especially around those nightly jobs.
00:04:39 Jordan: Billing is usage-based for Hosted, and for Dedicated it's a combination: committed monthly capacity + overage for burst use. We can model your nightly job consumption and recommend reserved node counts or a reservation with burst credits to smooth billing.
00:04:55 Priya: Can we reserve mixed card types? Our batch is fine on A100s but interactive needs H100 for latency.
00:05:01 Maya: Mixed pools are supported — you can reserve a tiered pool and route interactive requests to faster instances. We also support model partitioning and kernel selection so the runtime picks the best card.
00:05:12 Ethan: Quick qual: what's your SLA for p99 latency on Dedicated?
00:05:17 Liam: SLAs vary by commitment; we typically offer 99.9% uptime and latency SLOs tied to instance types. For tight p99 latency guarantees we recommend Dedicated with warm pools and prewarmed KV cache. SLA details we can include in the contract.
00:05:30 Priya: How invasive is Private deployment to our network? Do you need open egress to Redwood control plane?
00:05:36 Maya: Private control plane can be air-gapped with periodic artifact transfers, or VPC-peered with restricted egress to our control plane. For fully on-prem we ship an appliance bundle and integrate with your KMS/HSM. We try to minimize egress by streaming telemetry via your SIEM.
00:05:52 Ethan: We have a compliance board that will want to see key rotation: can we rotate keys without downtime?
00:05:57 Maya: Yes, KMS-backed keys allow rotation with zero-downtime if you use envelope encryption. We can walk Alex through the KMS integration flow in the follow-up.
00:06:07 Jordan: I'm going to share a rough sizing thought: based on 200 concurrent interactive users at 2k tokens/req and target p95 250ms, you likely need 8–12 H100-equivalent instances reserved with a 2-node hot-pool for immediate spikes, plus reserved A100s for batch. This is a starting point, we'll refine once Maya has the perf profile.
00:06:29 Ethan: That's helpful. Can you also include an option for a short pilot — like 2 weeks — where we run a mirrored workload to validate tail latency and cost?
00:06:38 Jordan: Definitely. We usually do a pilot with an SRE-run benchmark. Maya will own the benchmarking plan.
00:06:44 Maya: I'll draft a plan: 3 model variants, 1k/5k/20k token traces, 30-minute storm windows, sample batch job replay. That'll give us warm/cold latencies and cost-per-token.
00:06:58 Priya: For success criteria, we need p95 <300ms for interactive and nightly batch completion within our existing job window (2 hours). Also cost per 1M tokens under $X — we'll confirm internal threshold.
00:07:11 Samir: Timeline? Ideally pilot in Q3. We need procurement and security signoff though.
00:07:17 Jordan: Sounds reasonable. Procurement tends to take 2–4 weeks for enterprise, so let's aim to start pilot mid-August.
00:07:24 Ethan: Fine. Anything else on tenancy guardrails? We want per-team quotas and chaos-recovery runbooks.
00:07:30 Maya: Redwood Console can set per-route quotas and token budgets, and we provide playbooks for evicting or throttling lower priority tenants in surge. We'll share our recommended runbook.
00:07:41 Alex: On the ops side, what's observability like? Traces per request, token breakdown, costs?
00:07:46 Liam: We surface token-level breakdowns, p50/p95/p99 latencies, per-route cost, and model-level tracing. You can export traces to Datadog or your APM.
00:07:56 Priya: Great. Also want to confirm retention windows for logs for compliance — we need 12 months.
00:08:02 Maya: We can set retention on your account and ship to your S3 bucket or SIEM. For Private installations you control retention.
00:08:09 Ethan: Ok, let's go into a short demo of our expected spike pattern — Alex do you want to share the sheet?
00:08:14 Alex: Yeah I'll drop a link in chat — (link to spike pattern sheet)
00:08:19 Jordan: We'll review that in the benchmark plan.
00:08:22 (---- 20 minutes of technical Q&A and brief whiteboarding around capacity math; portions transcribed imperfectly, some speaker labels generic)
00:28:30 Speaker 1: so if we assume 3k tokens per interactive session at peak 600 concurrent it's roughly 1.8 million tokens per minute which maps to about X instances — need the kernel math —
00:29:02 Maya: (laugh) yes the kernel math can be rough but we'll model it; we also look at sequence length distribution not just average.
00:29:32 Priya: Another thought: can we do model multiplexing — have smaller models handle initial step and only promote to the big model for heavy ops?
00:29:41 Liam: Absolutely — routing rules can do staged calls. That reduces cost and burst pressure.
00:29:55 Ethan: What about failure modes — if the hot pool is exhausted and hosted fallback is disabled, do we queue or error?
00:30:02 Maya: You can choose queueing policies with timeouts and circuit-breakers. For client facing interactive features we recommend queueing with exponential backoff and a fallback to cached results if latency thresholds exceeded.
00:30:12 Samir: Ok. Let's capture next steps and owners.
00:30:18 Jordan: Quick recap — we will: 1) Send pricing + security docs; 2) Maya will draft benchmark plan and env spec; 3) Schedule VPC/KMS deep dive with Alex and Priya; 4) Customer to confirm procurement path and internal cost threshold. Anything to add?
00:30:34 Ethan: Add 'confirm dataset redaction approach' — we may need to redact PHI before sending to any external service.
00:30:40 Priya: And add 'verify quantization A/B test results for clinical accuracy' to the plan.
00:30:46 Jordan: Noted. We'll include both in the plan.
00:30:50 (closing banter)
00:31:05 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and the plan.
00:31:10 Ethan: Thanks — appreciate it.
